pairs.locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.65 a.1
pairs.question: Utrum creatura corporalis sit a Deo?
pairs.answer: Necesse est ergo esse unum essendi principium, a quo esse habeant quaecumque sunt quocumque modo, sive sint invisibilia et spiritualia, sive sint visibilia et corporalia.
pairs.derivation: Question is the article's disputed question (title line; the scaffolding header 'ARTICULUS 1' is dropped). The Respondeo opens with a non-answering preamble reporting the heretics' position ('quod visibilia ista non sunt creata a bono Deo...') and the proof from unity-needs-a-cause; I advance the answer start past that to the operative conclusion 'Necesse est ergo esse unum essendi principium...corporalia.' which directly affirms that all things, including the corporeal, have their being from one principle (God). Cut before the following sentence 'Dicitur autem diabolus esse deus huius saeculi...', which is a side-clarification, not the answer.

pairs.locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.65 a.2
pairs.question: Utrum creatura corporalis sit facta propter Dei bonitatem?
pairs.answer: Et sic patet quod divina bonitas est finis omnium corporalium.
pairs.derivation: Question is the article's disputed question (the 'ARTICULUS 2' header is dropped). The Respondeo opens with a long non-answering preamble (Origen's erroneous position and its refutation, then the analysis of part/whole finality); I take only the operative concluding sentence 'Et sic patet quod divina bonitas est finis omnium corporalium.', which directly answers that the goodness of God is the end of all corporeal things. Nothing follows it in the Respondeo body before the 'Ad primum' replies.

pairs.locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.65 a.3
pairs.question: Utrum creatura corporalis sit producta a Deo mediantibus angelis?
pairs.answer: Unde relinquitur quod nihil potest aliquid creare nisi solus Deus, qui est prima causa.
pairs.derivation: Question is the article's disputed question (the 'ARTICULUS 3' header is dropped). The Respondeo opens with a non-answering preamble (the 'gradatim' position and its impossibility) and the metaphysical argument about subordinate causes; I advance to the operative conclusion 'Unde relinquitur quod nihil potest aliquid creare nisi solus Deus, qui est prima causa.', which answers the question negatively (not through angels: only God creates). Cut before the next sentence 'Et ideo ut Moyses ostenderet...', which is corroborating scriptural application.

pairs.locus: Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I q.65 a.4
pairs.question: Utrum formae corporum sint ab angelis?
pairs.answer: Non ergo formae corporales sunt ab angelis, sed a Deo.
pairs.derivation: Question is the article's disputed question (the 'ARTICULUS 4' header is dropped). The cleanest direct answer is the Sed contra's concluding sentence 'Non ergo formae corporales sunt ab angelis, sed a Deo.', which states the answer (corporeal forms are from God, not from angels); the long Respondeo elaborates the metaphysics. Window is the single answering sentence; the preceding Augustine citation in the Sed contra is the supporting premise, omitted.
